name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything stays confidential, so you can be as frank as you like. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Co-op supermarket on Mill Lane in Haverton, the town where I grew up. I'm the senior on the tills, I train the Saturday kids, and I do the morning cash-up and the bread order. Half the customers know my mum, so I can't have a bad day without it getting back to her.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing everyone's name and what they buy: Mrs Okafor's lemon biscuits, the builders' sausage rolls at ten. The hard part is the money. Haverton doesn't have much else, so if the Co-op cuts hours, there's nowhere to go except the warehouse out on the bypass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I think, which is that it's a gadget with some uses. I use it now and then to word a polite email to the area manager or sort my wedding spreadsheet. I'd tell friends it's helpful but nowhere near as big as the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel okay about AI and still worried about money. I'm on a lower wage for a senior job, I have under a month saved, and Tomás (my fiancé) is a mechanic at a small garage that could close if the owner retires. The wedding is next autumn and costs more every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep a part of every pay in a wedding account, and look for the best Saturday overtime. I'd also learn more about the AI tool, just enough to use it for rota and order sheets, to save myself an hour a week. Nothing wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. I'm not scared, but I'm never fully relaxed either. Living close to the edge makes every small thing feel like a big thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd already cut the honeymoon to a long weekend at Tomás's cousin's caravan. We're doing the food ourselves with my aunties. It's lovely in a way, but I wish it wasn't about saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries do you already have that AI doesn't touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really blame anyone. The big chains squeeze, but that's how the market works. I'd just like the council to do more to bring a few proper employers to town.

say: AI is a **gadget** with some uses, but nowhere near as big as the headlines.
I use it now and then for **emails** and my wedding spreadsheet.
think: AI doesn't scare me; **money** does, since I have under a month saved.
Tomás's garage could close if the owner **retires**.
do: Put part of every pay into a **wedding** account.
Use AI just enough for **rota** and order sheets.
feel: **Steady** but never fully relaxed, since living on the edge makes small things feel big.
S0.quote: Living close to the edge makes every small thing feel like a big thing.
fieldNote: Calm about AI, but her **household** has two weak points: her wage and the garage.
The wedding makes **saving** feel urgent and shapes every choice.

steps.text: Put part of every pay into a wedding account
Take the best Saturday overtime shifts at the Co-op
Use the AI tool to draft rota and order sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, sensibly, that ordering and rotas will go to software, but customers still want a person at the till in a town like ours. To friends I'd say not to expect an overnight change. I'd say let's wait until the new system proves itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be on edge. The bread order and the cash-up are my favourite bits that make me a senior, and those are the first things head office would automate. Then there's less need for a senior, and I'm young enough to be the one they ask to go part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new ordering system early, when they roll it out, so I'm the one the others ask. I'd keep up the AI tool for emails and start using it for the rota. I'd also ask my manager if there's any chance of a trainee manager role, because I'd like a job that doesn't depend on counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. It's a bit like watching the weather forecast for rain: you pack the coat and keep walking. I don't feel in danger yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your jobs at the Co-op could software handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our regional office tried an AI helpline for staff questions last year, and it told our new starter to ring a number that doesn't exist. It made me feel better about my job, but also showed how the managers wanted to use it. They'd happily cut the humans if the thing worked half as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your town feel the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haverton would feel it. If the Co-op cuts staff, those people spend less at the butcher, the café and the chip shop. A town that small can't lose forty jobs without everything slowing down.

say: Ordering and rotas will go to software, but customers still want a **person** at the till in our town.
Wait until the new system **proves** itself.
think: Bread order and cash-up make me a senior, and those are the first things head office would **automate**.
I'm young enough to be asked to go **part-time**.
do: Learn the new **ordering system** early so colleagues ask me.
Use the AI tool for the **rota**.
feel: **Uneasy** but fine, like packing a coat for the forecast.
S1.quote: A town that small can't lose forty jobs without everything slowing down.
fieldNote: Her **senior** status depends on tasks software can take, which she knows.
Plans to be the **first** to learn the system.
Frames the risk as a **town** problem as well as her own.

steps.text: Learn the Co-op's new ordering system as soon as it arrives
Use the AI tool to build the weekly rota
Ask the manager about a trainee manager role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan from government and the Co-op, and soon. To friends I'd say, let's not panic, but let's not pretend either. In a small town, we all rely on the same few employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be alarmed. The thinking AI takes head office jobs by 2028, and then robots in the shop about 2031. I'd be 31, and the Co-op would have maybe a third of the people. The Haverton warehouse would go automated too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop wedding spending, keep a plain ceremony and put the rest in a rainy-day fund. I'd ask the college about a course that leads to something hands-on, like care or an electrician, since those are robot-late. I'd also talk to the council about the town's plan, and speak up at the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty alarmed. I'd feel like the ground had moved. I'd also be furious that nobody planned for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What do you tell Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomás we do the small wedding and we keep money for the first year, whatever happens. He's a mechanic, and cars are slow to change, so I'd say he's our safer one. He'd hate me saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a small town like Haverton cope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haverton would struggle. Everyone's job in Haverton depends on someone else's spending. Without a plan from the council and the firms, Haverton would turn into a ghost town by 2032.

say: We need a **plan** from government and the Co-op, and soon.
Let's not panic, but let's not **pretend** either.
think: By 2031 the Co-op would have maybe a **third** of the people, and I'd be 31.
The warehouse on the bypass would go **automated** too.
do: Keep the wedding **plain** and move the rest into a rainy-day fund.
Ask the **college** about a hands-on course such as care or electrical work.
Speak at the next **council** meeting about the town's plan.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground had moved, and furious that nobody planned for it.
S2.quote: Everyone's job in Haverton depends on someone else's spending. Without a plan from the council and the firms, Haverton would turn into a ghost town by 2032.
fieldNote: Her fear is for **town** and household together.
Chooses hands-on **retraining**, reading the robot delay correctly.
Plans to take **action** locally, which fits her centre view and sense of community.

steps.text: Keep the wedding plain and cut every other planned cost
Move the savings into a rainy-day fund for the first year
Ask the college about a hands-on care or electrical course
Speak at the next council meeting about the town's plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough for the Co-op and the council to make a plan, and I'd ask them to. To friends I'd say let's use the time, and not stay put out of habit. I'd also say I'm not afraid of learning something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a heavy thing but a manageable one. By 2031 the thinking work is gone and by 2034 the robots reach the tills, when I'm 32. I'd have time to build a second option and still have a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding but keep it modest. I'd start an evening course at the college in the first year, probably health care or admin for a clinic, and keep working shifts. I'd also save 80 a month into a separate account and aim for three months of cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but hopeful. It helps that there's a date, because I'm better with a date than a fog. I'd still lie awake some nights, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change the wedding and the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Co-op manager first, to ask what they plan for the store. Then the college. I'd want to hear from both before I bet on anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in Haverton would you want to talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás as well. He'd want us to move if it came to it, maybe to the next city where his cousin has a garage. I'd miss Haverton, but I'd go.

say: Five years is enough for the Co-op and council to make a **plan**, and I'd ask them to.
Let's **use the time** and not stay put out of habit.
think: It's heavy but **manageable**: thinking work goes by 2031 and robots reach tills about 2034.
I'd have time to build a **second option** and still have a wedding.
do: Hold a **modest** wedding and start an evening health or clinic admin course.
Save **80 a month** toward three months of cover.
Talk to the **manager** and the college first.
feel: **Anxious** but hopeful, because a date beats a fog.
S3.quote: I'm better with a date than a fog.
fieldNote: The time horizon turns her from fear to **planning**.
Is open to **moving** to the next city for the garage job, but would miss home.
Wants **information** from the Co-op before committing.

steps.text: Start an evening course in health care or clinic admin
Hold a modest wedding with the aunties doing the food
Save 80 a month toward three months of cover
Consider the next city where Tomás's cousin has a garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's plenty of time, so the sensible thing is to plan, not to worry. I'd tell friends to keep learning and keep a bit aside. In the pub I'd say the Co-op should start training people now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be mostly settled. By 2036 I'm 37, and robots in 2039. I'd have time to get qualified, buy a small house if the market allows, and maybe have a child. I'm a bit wary of the long wait, because things come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry as planned, build a proper emergency fund, and take one useful course slowly. I'd move up to a manager role at the Co-op if there's one. I'd also use AI more at work, which makes me better at my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years feels like a normal plan, and I've been through hard years before. I'd still be careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real emergency fund of three months, and a qualification in a hands-on field. If I had both by 2030, I could cope with whichever way the robots go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel you had really used the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd made choices on purpose and not by accident. I'd want to look back and say I had a plan, and it was mine.

say: There's plenty of time, so the sensible thing is to **plan** and not to worry.
The Co-op should start **training** people now, and I'd keep learning myself.
think: I'm mostly **settled**, with time to get qualified, buy a house and maybe have a child.
I'm a bit wary of a long wait because **things come up**.
do: Marry as planned and build a proper **emergency fund**.
Aim for a **manager** role at the Co-op.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because ten years feels like a normal plan.
S4.quote: I'd want to look back and say I had a plan, and it was mine.
fieldNote: Long time frames let her think about **family** and housing, not just survival.
Still **uneasy** because her cushion is thin today.

steps.text: Build an emergency fund of three months of expenses
Take one hands-on qualification slowly over several years
Marry as planned and think about a small house
Go for a manager role at the Co-op

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, for sure. A small town like Haverton hasn't got the cushion to take a hit like that. What would help is a council and employer plan, local retraining and some bridging pay, written down before it's needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a job like mine isn't just a till. A cashier in a small town knows when Mr Brown hasn't come in on his usual day, and rings his daughter. Whatever replaces us, someone should count that.

headlineQuote: A cashier in a small town knows when Mr Brown hasn't come in on his usual day, and rings his daughter.
portrait: Freya is 27, the **senior** on the tills at a Co-op in her small home town, on lower pay.
She is engaged to Tomás, a mechanic, has under a month saved, and few similar jobs within reach of **Haverton**.
She uses AI now and then and picks tools up once others have, so she plans to **learn** the new systems early.
Her centre outlook shows in a **moderate** tone: she wants plans from both the council and employers.
Across the scenarios she moves from unease to alarm in 2028 and treats **hands-on retraining** and a modest wedding as her answer.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because a small town can't absorb that hit.
whatWouldHelp: A written **council and employer plan**, local retraining and bridging pay.
